item.title: New build slowdown deals fresh blow to government’s 1.5m homes pledge
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government’s target of building 1.5 million new homes during this Parliament faces growing challenges, as latest industry figures reveal a continued slowdown in construction starts. According to the National House Building Council (NHBC), registrations for new homes fell by 4% year-on-year in Q2 2026, marking the second consecutive quarterly decline.

Economic headwinds dampen construction

Housebuilders registered just 29,162 new properties between April and June 2026, down from 30,259 in the same period last year. Industry experts attribute this slowdown to multiple factors including high interest rates, rising construction costs and ongoing economic uncertainty. These pressures have led many developers to scale back their building programmes.

Daniel Pearce, NHBC’s Chief Strategy Officer, noted: “Affordability constraints continue to impact buyer demand, while builders face their own financial challenges. The decline in registrations reflects these market conditions.” The figures emerge as Housing Secretary Angela Rayner publicly acknowledged the difficulties in meeting Labour’s ambitious housing targets.

Regional variations in construction activity

The slowdown has affected different parts of the UK unevenly. Half of the country’s regions saw fewer registrations compared to Q2 2025, with particularly sharp declines in:

  • South West (-42%)
  • East Midlands (-36%)
  • Wales (-34%)

London bucked the trend with a 170% surge in registrations, though NHBC cautioned that the capital’s figures tend to fluctuate more due to the nature of large-scale developments. Other regions showing growth included the North West (+37%) and East of England (+15%).

Pearce welcomed the government’s commitment to council housebuilding, stating: “The proposed social housing programme could significantly boost supply if properly funded. The industry also needs planning reforms and reduced regulatory burdens to help meet housing targets.”

With construction starts continuing to lag behind targets, questions remain about how quickly the housing shortfall can be addressed. Prospective buyers and those looking to move may wish to monitor local market conditions closely, as availability of new properties varies considerably by region.

item.title: Propertymark urges estate agents to get qualified before reforms
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The property sector is poised for significant changes as the UK government moves forward with reforms aimed at modernising the homebuying and selling process. Among the key proposals is the introduction of mandatory qualifications for estate and letting agents across England, Wales, and Northern Ireland. Propertymark, a leading professional body, is urging agents to take proactive steps and gain qualifications ahead of these regulatory changes, rather than waiting for them to become compulsory.

A Push for Higher Standards

The government’s plans include publishing a non-statutory Code of Practice later this year, with a consultation on mandatory qualifications scheduled for 2027. These reforms, which build on recommendations made by the Regulation of Property Agents (RoPA) Working Group in 2019, aim to enhance the speed and reliability of property transactions while raising professional standards across the industry. Propertymark has long advocated for these changes, viewing them as essential for increasing consumer trust and improving the overall experience of buying and selling homes.

Propertymark’s members already adhere to recognised qualifications, a code of conduct, and independent regulation on a voluntary basis. However, with mandatory qualifications on the horizon, the organisation is encouraging all agents to prepare early. Nathan Emerson, CEO of Propertymark, emphasised the importance of acting now, stating that gaining qualifications demonstrates a commitment to higher standards and positions agents as trusted professionals in an increasingly competitive market.

Growing Demand for Professional Qualifications

The push for qualifications comes amid growing demand from both consumers and industry professionals. In 2025 alone, nearly 3,500 new learners registered for Propertymark courses, over 7,400 examinations were completed, and 1,500 qualifications were awarded. This surge highlights the increasing recognition of the value of professional development in the property sector.

For estate agents, investing in qualifications now could provide a competitive edge, particularly as consumers become more aware of the importance of working with qualified professionals. Propertymark’s efforts to promote higher standards have resonated with buyers and sellers alike, reinforcing the need for agents to demonstrate their expertise and commitment to ethical practices.

Whilst the government’s consultation on mandatory qualifications is still a few years away, agents might consider taking advantage of the current momentum to upskill and align themselves with industry best practices. By doing so, they can not only enhance their own credibility but also contribute to a more transparent and efficient property market.

As the sector evolves, estate agents who embrace these changes early are likely to be well-positioned to navigate the new landscape and meet the expectations of increasingly discerning consumers.

item.title: Property sales market steadies while rental pressure builds
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK housing market showed signs of stabilisation in May, with property sales becoming more balanced whilst rental pressures intensified, according to Propertymark's latest Housing Insight Report. The data reveals a modest improvement in sales stock levels alongside cooling buyer demand, creating better conditions for purchasers. Meanwhile, the lettings market continues to grapple with severe supply shortages, with eight prospective tenants now competing for each available rental property.

Sales Market Finds Equilibrium

May brought welcome relief for homebuyers as property choice improved across the UK. The average estate agency branch reported 44 properties available for sale – a slight increase from previous months. At the same time, new buyer registrations dipped to 64 per branch, suggesting demand is softening from its recent peaks.

This gradual rebalancing means purchasers now face less competition when making offers. Properties are typically selling below asking price, with transactions taking over four months to complete from offer acceptance to exchange. Industry experts attribute this cautious approach to ongoing affordability challenges, despite the Bank of England maintaining interest rates at 5.25%.

Rental Market Squeeze Intensifies

The lettings sector presents a starkly different picture, with supply failing to meet growing tenant demand. Available rental properties fell to just 12 per branch in May, whilst the number of prospective tenants increased. This imbalance leaves eight applicants chasing each rental home – maintaining the intense competition seen throughout 2024.

The only positive note came from rent arrears, which showed slight improvement with just 2.1% of letting agents reporting payment issues. Propertymark's CEO Nathan Emerson commented: "The long-standing imbalance between supply and demand remains firmly in place in the lettings sector. Although tenant demand increased during May, available stock fell slightly, maintaining the unsustainable pressure on renters."

As the summer market develops, homeowners considering selling may find more favourable conditions emerging, whilst renters continue to face one of the most challenging markets in recent memory. The contrasting fortunes of these two sectors highlight the complex dynamics shaping Britain's housing landscape.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK property and mortgage sectors are experiencing significant leadership changes, with key roles at BNP Paribas Real Estate UK and the Conveyancing Association (CA) undergoing transitions. These shifts aim to ensure continuity, stability, and a focus on strategic priorities during periods of restructuring and evolution.

BNP Paribas Real Estate UK Leadership Restructuring

Mark England, chief executive of BNP Paribas Real Estate UK, is stepping down after nearly four decades with the company. Whilst he will remain as a senior adviser during the transition, Gary Higgins, managing director of subsidiary Strutt & Parker, has been appointed as interim chief executive. Higgins brings over 20 years of experience with BNP Paribas, having joined Strutt & Parker in April 2025.

The leadership restructuring is part of a broader initiative to ensure an experienced management team is in place. Jean-Maxime Jouis, chief executive of BNP Paribas Real Estate, emphasised that the new structure combines proven leadership, UK market expertise, and international insight. This approach aims to maintain continuity and stability whilst delivering on the company’s strategic goals.

Conveyancing Association Chair Steps Down

Meanwhile, the Conveyancing Association has announced that Nicky Heathcote, its non-executive chair, will step down at the end of her second term. Heathcote will remain in the role until a successor is appointed to ensure a smooth transition. During her tenure, she oversaw the introduction of a new governance framework and a member-focused strategy, whilst representing the sector in government consultations aimed at improving the home buying and selling process.

Heathcote will continue her involvement in the sector as chair of the PCCB Compliance Committee and a member of the Women in Conveyancing Committee. Additionally, David Hodgson, treasurer and founding board member, is also stepping down. Recruitment for both positions is currently underway, with the CA seeking individuals to guide the association through its next phase.

What These Changes Mean for the Industry

Leadership transitions in prominent organisations like BNP Paribas Real Estate UK and the Conveyancing Association often signal a period of reflection and renewal. For homeowners and prospective buyers, these changes could lead to enhanced processes and greater efficiency in the property market. Borrowers might consider staying informed about developments in these organisations, as they could influence the broader landscape of property transactions.

As the property and mortgage sectors continue to evolve, the focus remains on delivering stability and improving the experience for all stakeholders. These leadership changes highlight the importance of experienced guidance in navigating complex markets and achieving long-term goals.

item.title: HMRC nets £100m in landlord tax crackdown
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) collected over £100m in unpaid taxes from landlords during the 2025-26 financial year, according to new data. The figures, obtained by accountancy firm Price Bailey, reveal this marks the third consecutive year where recoveries have surpassed the £100m threshold, with the latest total reaching £104.3m – nearly triple the £36.8m collected in 2019-20.

Increased scrutiny on rental income

HMRC has significantly expanded its use of property data to identify landlords who may have underreported rental income. Land Registry records now help pinpoint owners of multiple residential properties who haven’t declared all taxable earnings. The tax authority has sent thousands of “nudge letters” encouraging voluntary disclosures, resulting in 11,511 landlords coming forward through the Let Property Campaign – the highest participation since 2018-19. The average disclosure involved £9,063 in unpaid tax.

Accountancy experts note that accidental landlords frequently find themselves caught in HMRC’s net. These include individuals who retained properties after moving in with partners, inherited homes, or temporarily relocated abroad. Many may not realise they need to declare rental profits, particularly if their lettings generate modest income.

Tax compliance challenges for landlords

The distinction between capital and revenue expenditure continues to cause confusion among property investors. While basic replacements (like-for-like kitchen refurbishments) typically qualify as tax-deductible expenses, substantial upgrades (installing a luxury kitchen where a standard one previously existed) may not receive the same treatment.

Recent tax changes have added further complexity:

  • Making Tax Digital for Income Tax will require quarterly reporting from April 2026 for landlords with combined property and self-employment income above £50,000 (threshold reducing to £20,000 from April 2028)
  • Capital Gains Tax annual exemption reduced to £3,000
  • Higher CGT rates applied to residential property sales
  • Corporation tax rates between 19% and 25% for limited company landlords

Andrew Park, tax investigations partner at Price Bailey, warned: “HMRC’s data-matching capabilities have become relentless. Most disclosures now follow nudge letters, with the tax authority pursuing larger volumes of smaller cases.”

With HMRC intensifying its property tax crackdown, landlords may wish to review their records carefully or seek professional advice to ensure full compliance with evolving regulations.

item.title: Home charging tax break widens property divide
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government’s recent announcement to eliminate VAT on domestic electricity bills for six months, starting in October, has sparked debate about its impact on electric vehicle (EV) owners. While households with driveways stand to benefit significantly, those reliant on public charging points may face higher costs, highlighting a growing divide in accessibility and affordability for EV users.

The VAT Reduction and Its Implications

Under the new policy, the current 5% VAT rate on domestic electricity will be removed temporarily, reducing the cost of charging EVs at home. Industry estimates suggest that drivers using off-peak home charging tariffs could see their running costs fall to as low as 1.5p per mile. This change is expected to make home charging even more economical, particularly for homeowners with private driveways.

However, the benefits are not universal. Public charging points remain subject to a 20% VAT rate, meaning drivers without access to off-street parking could pay significantly more—up to 16p to 20p per mile, depending on the charger and vehicle type. This disparity has led to calls for the government to equalise VAT rates across both domestic and public charging options, ensuring a fairer transition to electric mobility.

Impact on Property and Accessibility

The VAT reduction has also drawn attention to the role of property features, such as driveways, in the adoption of EVs. For many buyers and renters, access to off-street parking is becoming a key consideration, as it directly affects the affordability and convenience of EV ownership. Households without private parking face not only higher charging costs but also limited alternatives, potentially discouraging them from making the switch to electric vehicles.

Industry groups have warned that the latest tax changes risk exacerbating existing inequalities. Tanya Sinclair, chief executive of Electric Vehicles UK, emphasised that millions of drivers without driveways are unfairly penalised, paying 20% VAT for the same electricity that home chargers can access tax-free. She called for a fairer approach to ensure all EV users can benefit from the transition to cleaner transport.

Calls for Policy Change

The RAC has echoed these concerns, urging the government to reconsider VAT rates on public charging. Simon Williams, head of policy at the RAC, highlighted the importance of affordability in encouraging widespread EV adoption. Lowering VAT on public charging could help level the playing field, enabling more households to embrace electric motoring without facing disproportionate costs.

As the UK moves towards its net-zero targets, addressing these disparities will be crucial. Ensuring that EV ownership is accessible and affordable for all, regardless of property type or location, could play a significant role in achieving a fair and inclusive transition to sustainable transport.

For homeowners considering the switch to electric vehicles, access to off-street charging remains a key factor. Meanwhile, policymakers may wish to explore further measures to support those reliant on public infrastructure, ensuring the benefits of EV ownership are shared equally.

item.title: Burnham slams door on stamp duty reform
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has confirmed the government will not introduce stamp duty reforms in this year’s Budget, ending speculation about potential changes to the property tax. The announcement may disappoint housing market professionals who have long argued the current system creates barriers for homeowners looking to move.

Stamp duty reform ruled out

When questioned about possible stamp duty changes, the prime minister stated unequivocally: “That won’t be happening.” The Treasury collected £16.6bn from stamp duty land tax last year, making it a substantial revenue stream that the government appears reluctant to alter. Burnham emphasised that large-scale tax reforms were not currently under consideration, though he reiterated the government’s commitment to creating a fairer tax system overall.

Property industry figures have frequently criticised stamp duty for discouraging homeowners from downsizing, relocating for work or otherwise moving house when their circumstances change. Some experts suggest this reduces the efficient use of housing stock across the country. However, with public finances under pressure from multiple demands – including an ageing population and defence commitments – the government seems focused on maintaining this significant income source.

Taxation priorities and property market implications

While ruling out stamp duty changes, the prime minister has previously acknowledged that some taxes may need to rise to meet growing expenditure needs. However, Labour’s election manifesto committed not to increase income tax, National Insurance or VAT rates – the three largest contributors to Treasury coffers.

For potential homebuyers and those considering a move, the confirmation means stamp duty calculations will remain unchanged for now. Homeowners thinking about relocating might wish to factor in the existing stamp duty rates when planning their finances. Mortgage borrowers may also want to consider how these costs affect their overall moving budget and property choices.

The property market will continue operating under the current stamp duty framework, with first-time buyers still benefiting from relief on properties up to £425,000 in England and Northern Ireland. While reform hopes have been dashed for this Budget, the debate about stamp duty’s impact on housing mobility seems likely to continue.

item.title: Revealed: The cities where agents are busiest
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New research highlights significant regional variations in letting agent workloads across Britain, with Nottingham emerging as the city where agencies handle the highest volume of rental properties. The Propoly study analysed rental listings across 21 major cities, revealing stark differences in market activity levels.

Nottingham leads in rental property volumes

The research found Nottingham letting agents manage more than twice the national average, with each agency handling 31.4 available properties. This compares to an overall UK average of 13.1 listings per agency. The city's 98 letting agents were marketing 3,078 rental properties during the study period in July 2026.

Newcastle ranked second with 23.5 properties per agency, followed by Aberdeen (18.2), Birmingham (17.2) and Leeds (16.5). Several other cities also recorded above-average activity levels, including:

  • Plymouth (15.6 listings per agency)
  • Bournemouth (15.3)
  • Leicester (15.1)
  • Portsmouth (15.1)
  • Sheffield (14.9)

London and other cities show lower activity

Despite having the largest rental market in absolute terms, London fell below the national average with just 12.2 properties per agency. The capital's 33,473 available rentals were spread across an estimated 2,744 agencies. Cardiff matched London's average, while Manchester recorded 10 listings per agency.

The lowest activity levels were found in:

  • Glasgow (8.0 listings per agency)
  • Newport (6.8)

Sim Sekhon, group CEO at Propoly, noted: "The volume of rental stock that letting agents are managing varies dramatically across the country, creating very different operational challenges in each market."

By Nadya Putri Maharani

New research highlights significant regional variations in letting agent workloads across Britain, with Nottingham emerging as the city where agencies handle the highest volume of rental properties. The Propoly study analysed rental listings across 21 major cities, revealing stark differences in market activity levels.

Nottingham leads in rental property volumes

The research found Nottingham letting agents manage more than twice the national average, with each agency handling 31.4 available properties. This compares to an overall UK average of 13.1 listings per agency. The city's 98 letting agents were marketing 3,078 rental properties during the study period in July 2026.

Newcastle ranked second with 23.5 properties per agency, followed by Aberdeen (18.2), Birmingham (17.2) and Leeds (16.5). Several other cities also recorded above-average activity levels, including:

  • Plymouth (15.6 listings per agency)
  • Bournemouth (15.3)
  • Leicester (15.1)
  • Portsmouth (15.1)
  • Sheffield (14.9)

London and other cities show lower activity

Despite having the largest rental market in absolute terms, London fell below the national average with just 12.2 properties per agency. The capital's 33,473 available rentals were spread across an estimated 2,744 agencies. Cardiff matched London's average, while Manchester recorded 10 listings per agency.

The lowest activity levels were found in:

  • Glasgow (8.0 listings per agency)
  • Newport (6.8)

Sim Sekhon, group CEO at Propoly, noted: "The volume of rental stock that letting agents are managing varies dramatically across the country, creating very different operational challenges in each market."

For renters, these findings suggest property availability and agent workloads vary considerably by location. Those searching in busier markets may encounter agents handling larger portfolios, whilst quieter areas could offer more dedicated service.

item.title: Time running out to shape major reform as consultation closes today
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The Financial Conduct Authority's (FCA) consultation period on potential mortgage lending reforms concludes today, with industry stakeholders having their final chance to shape what could become significant changes to UK home financing rules. The proposed adjustments aim to create more flexible affordability assessments, potentially benefiting first-time buyers, self-employed individuals and older applicants who often face hurdles in the current system.

Key proposals under consideration

The regulator's suggestions include several noteworthy changes that could modernise mortgage lending practices:

  • More accommodating approaches for borrowers with fluctuating incomes
  • Improved access for applicants earning in foreign currencies
  • Greater emphasis on current financial circumstances rather than past credit issues

These reforms could make homeownership achievable for more people while maintaining responsible lending standards. Industry experts have largely welcomed the direction of travel, though some caution that the proposals represent only part of the solution.

The importance of early financial preparation

Tom Eyre of Loqbox acknowledges the positive intent behind the FCA's proposals but highlights a crucial gap in the approach. He suggests that while assessing borrowers' current situations rather than historical credit problems represents progress, many potential homeowners need support long before they reach the mortgage application stage.

Eyre points out that the UK system often expects individuals to make their largest financial commitment with minimal preparation. Some consumers avoid credit entirely to remain "sensible", only to discover that having no credit history can be as problematic as having a poor one when applying for a mortgage.

The financial wellbeing expert advocates for a more gradual approach to mortgage readiness, with earlier interventions to help people build robust credit profiles over time. Without this, he warns, easier access to mortgages might simply shift financial difficulties from the application stage to later repayment challenges.

As the consultation closes, the mortgage industry awaits the FCA's next steps. While the proposed changes could help many borrowers, the broader conversation about financial preparation and education continues to evolve alongside regulatory developments.

item.title: The £1m crime wave that hit new-build sites
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A criminal gang responsible for stealing over £1 million worth of appliances from new-build homes across England has been sentenced to prison terms following a major police investigation. The four men admitted to targeting nearly 450 properties in 10 counties during a nine-month crime spree, leaving behind significant damage and safety hazards for homeowners and developers.

Nationwide burglary operation uncovered

Hertfordshire Constabulary led Operation Linkage, a coordinated effort to track the organised crime group that systematically raided housing developments between January and October 2025. The burglars typically gained entry by smashing windows before removing boilers, heat pumps and other valuable fixtures. Their activities spanned Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Gloucestershire and seven other counties, with some targeted properties already sold to buyers awaiting completion.

Detective Constable Tilly Andrews, the investigating officer, noted the considerable impact on both developers and prospective homeowners. The thefts not only caused financial losses but also created dangerous conditions, with exposed gas and water pipes left behind after equipment removal. The complex investigation required collaboration between multiple police forces and housing developers across England.

Sentences handed down at St Albans Crown Court

The four defendants – all aged between 19 and 26 and from Northampton and London – received prison terms ranging from 47 months to 58 months after pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit burglary. Dinis Cibotari, 24, received the longest sentence of four years and two months. Their convictions follow forensic work that linked the gang to crimes across multiple regions.

For those purchasing new-build properties, this case highlights the importance of checking what security measures developers have in place during construction and before handover. Homeowners might consider asking about alarm systems, site security protocols and whether properties are insured during the construction phase. Some developers may offer additional protection services for buyers awaiting completion.

While this sentencing brings closure to affected parties, it serves as a reminder of the vulnerabilities that can exist during property development stages. The police operation demonstrates how coordinated efforts can successfully tackle organised crime targeting the housing sector.

item.title: Growing threat of tenant fraud
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords across the UK are facing increasing challenges with tenant fraud, according to recent research. False information on rental applications and deceptive financial claims are becoming more prevalent, leaving property owners vulnerable to significant financial losses. With the private rental sector under pressure, experts suggest thorough tenant vetting has never been more crucial.

The rising risk of fraudulent applications

Industry reports indicate a noticeable uptick in misleading or entirely fabricated details on tenancy applications. Common issues include inflated income claims, falsified employment records, and even stolen identities being used to secure properties. Some applicants are going as far as submitting doctored bank statements or payslips to appear more financially stable than they truly are.

For landlords, the consequences can be severe. Tenants who misrepresent their financial situation may struggle to meet rental payments, leading to potential arrears and costly eviction processes. In some cases, properties have suffered significant damage when occupied by fraudulent tenants who disappear without trace.

Protecting against rental fraud

Property owners might consider several protective measures to mitigate these risks:

  • Comprehensive reference checks including previous landlords and employers
  • Verification of financial documents directly with banks or employers
  • Use of professional tenant referencing services
  • Consideration of rent guarantee insurance
  • Checking applicants against tenancy fraud databases

Many letting agents now recommend conducting face-to-face interviews where possible, as this can help identify inconsistencies in an applicant's story. Digital verification tools are also becoming more sophisticated, with some services cross-referencing application details against multiple data sources.

The private rental market remains competitive in many areas, which may tempt some applicants to embellish their credentials. However, landlords who invest time in thorough vetting processes could potentially save themselves from considerable financial headaches down the line.

item.title: Nearly two-thirds of professional landlords raising rents
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent research indicates that nearly two-thirds of professional landlords in the UK have increased rents over the past year, with rising operational costs and regulatory changes cited as key factors. This trend reflects broader pressures in the private rental sector, where landlords are adjusting their strategies to maintain profitability.

Why landlords are increasing rents

Several financial pressures are contributing to higher rents across the private rental market. Many landlords report facing:

  • Higher mortgage rates on buy-to-let properties
  • Increased maintenance and repair costs
  • Growing regulatory compliance expenses
  • Changes to tax relief on mortgage interest

These rising costs have led many professional landlords to review their rental pricing structures. Whilst some have absorbed part of these increases, others have passed them on to tenants through higher monthly payments.

The impact on the rental market

The research suggests these rent increases are influencing tenant behaviour and landlord investment decisions. Some tenants may find themselves priced out of certain areas or property types, potentially leading to increased demand for more affordable housing options.

For landlords, the changing financial landscape appears to be prompting strategic shifts:

  • Some are reconsidering their property portfolios
  • Others are exploring ways to improve energy efficiency to meet new standards
  • A proportion may be looking at alternative investment strategies

Prospective renters might find it helpful to research local market conditions and be prepared for potential rent reviews when renewing tenancies. Those concerned about affordability could consider exploring different areas or property types where rental growth may be less pronounced.

As the rental market continues to evolve, both landlords and tenants face new challenges in balancing affordability with sustainable property investment.

item.title: The tale of two mayors…
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent research has revealed striking differences in housing market performance between London and Greater Manchester under their respective mayors, Sadiq Khan and Andy Burnham. The comparative analysis highlights how regional policies and economic factors have shaped contrasting property trends in these two major UK cities.

Diverging property market trajectories

The study suggests London's housing market has experienced slower growth under Mayor Khan's tenure, with average property prices increasing by just 12% since 2016. Meanwhile, Greater Manchester has seen prices surge by 28% during the same period under Mayor Burnham's leadership. This divergence appears linked to several key factors:

  • More aggressive housing targets and development incentives in Greater Manchester
  • London's higher stamp duty rates potentially dampening market activity
  • Greater affordability driving demand in Manchester's surrounding boroughs
  • Differing approaches to planning permission and brownfield site development

Policy impacts on affordability and supply

The research also examines how each mayor's housing policies have affected local affordability and supply. London has focused more on affordable housing quotas and rent controls, while Greater Manchester has prioritised increasing overall housing stock through strategic partnerships with developers.

First-time buyers in Manchester may have benefited from the region's faster-growing supply of new homes, with completions increasing 37% since 2017 compared to London's 22% rise. However, some analysts note that Manchester's rapid growth brings its own challenges, including infrastructure pressures in popular commuter towns.

For homeowners and investors tracking these markets, the research underscores how regional leadership can significantly influence local property dynamics. Those considering purchases in either region might wish to examine how current policies could affect long-term value and rental potential.

As both cities continue to evolve their housing strategies, market watchers will be keen to see whether these divergent trends persist or begin to converge in coming years.

item.title: Tenant demand strengthens 2.3%
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK rental market has shown signs of resilience in the second quarter of this year, with tenant demand rising by 2.3%. This uptick reflects a growing appetite for rental properties across England, as nearly one in three listings were marked as let agreed during this period.

Rising Demand in the Rental Sector

The increase in tenant demand highlights the continued strength of the rental market, despite broader economic challenges. With many households opting to rent rather than buy, landlords and property investors may find opportunities in this buoyant sector. The data suggests that rental properties are being snapped up quickly, indicating a competitive landscape for tenants.

Regional Variations and Market Trends

Whilst the overall trend points to growing demand, regional variations are likely to play a role in how this impacts the market. Urban areas, in particular, may see heightened competition due to their appeal to young professionals and students. Meanwhile, suburban and rural locations could also experience increased interest as tenants seek more space and affordability.

For landlords, this surge in demand could translate into stable rental income and potentially higher yields. However, it’s essential to stay informed about local market conditions and tenant preferences to remain competitive. Keeping properties well-maintained and offering flexible tenancy terms might help attract and retain tenants in this dynamic environment.

Implications for Tenants and Investors

For tenants, the rising demand may lead to tighter competition for available properties, especially in popular areas. As a result, they might need to act quickly when suitable listings arise and ensure their applications are thorough and well-prepared.

For property investors, the strengthening rental market could present a favourable opportunity to expand portfolios or optimise existing assets. Conducting thorough research into local demand trends and rental yields is crucial for making informed decisions. Additionally, staying compliant with evolving regulations, such as energy efficiency standards, will be key to maintaining a successful rental business.

As the rental market continues to evolve, both tenants and landlords will need to adapt to changing dynamics. Keeping a close eye on market trends and seeking professional advice where necessary could help navigate this competitive landscape effectively.

item.title: Investors urged to respond to smart data consultation
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property professionals and investors are being encouraged to share their insights on the government’s smart data consultation, which closes on 1 October. The initiative, spearheaded by the Open Property Data Association (OPDA), aims to gather feedback from stakeholders to shape the future of property data usage in the UK. With smart data playing an increasingly pivotal role in the property market, this consultation represents a key opportunity for industry experts to influence policy and innovation.

What is the smart data consultation?

The government’s smart data consultation focuses on how data can be used more effectively to improve transparency, efficiency, and decision-making in the property sector. Smart data refers to the secure sharing of information between organisations, enabling consumers, businesses, and regulators to access accurate and timely insights. For property professionals, this could mean streamlined processes, reduced costs, and enhanced trust in transactions.

The consultation seeks to address challenges such as data fragmentation, privacy concerns, and the need for standardised practices. By gathering input from industry stakeholders, the government hopes to create a framework that balances innovation with consumer protection.

Why is participation important?

For property investors and professionals, engaging with this consultation could have far-reaching implications. The outcomes could influence how data is collected, shared, and utilised across the sector, potentially reshaping the way transactions are conducted. Key areas of focus include:

  • Improving access to property data for buyers, sellers, and renters.
  • Enhancing transparency in pricing and property valuations.
  • Reducing inefficiencies in processes such as conveyancing and mortgage applications.

By contributing to the consultation, stakeholders can help ensure that the final framework aligns with the needs of the property market while fostering innovation and competition.

How to get involved

Property professionals who wish to participate in the consultation can submit their responses via the government’s official website. The OPDA has emphasised the importance of providing detailed feedback, particularly on issues such as data security, interoperability, and the potential benefits of smart data for consumers and businesses. With the deadline fast approaching, those interested are encouraged to act promptly to ensure their voices are heard.

As the property sector continues to evolve, the smart data consultation represents a critical step towards creating a more efficient and transparent market. By engaging with this initiative, investors and professionals can play a role in shaping the future of property data in the UK.

item.title: No Rent Freeze in England—but New Restrictions on Rents and Rent Increases
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government has confirmed it won't introduce rent controls in England, despite calls from tenant advocacy groups. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner stated on BBC Breakfast that evidence from other regions showed rent freezes don't "necessarily bring rents down". Instead, ministers are relying on new regulations under the Renters' Rights Act to create fairer conditions for tenants whilst maintaining landlord protections.

New Advertising and Payment Rules

From 1st May 2026, landlords must include a 'proposed rent' in all property advertisements (excluding traditional 'to let' boards). This figure becomes the legally binding rent when the tenancy begins. The rules aim to prevent rental bidding wars, with local councils empowered to issue civil penalties of up to £7,000 for violations including:

  • Failing to display a proposed rent
  • Encouraging or accepting offers above the advertised rate
  • Suggesting willingness to consider higher rents

Additional payment restrictions prohibit landlords from taking advance rent before tenancy agreements are signed, with £5,000 penalties for breaches. The only permitted advance payment is one month's rent, and only after contracts are signed but before the tenancy starts.

Tenant Protections During Tenancies

The legislation introduces several safeguards for renters after moving in:

  • Tenants may request an 'open market rent determination' within six months of a new tenancy if they believe their rent exceeds local market rates
  • All assured tenancies automatically become periodic, aligning rental periods with payment cycles
  • Landlords cannot demand rent payments earlier than the first day of each rental period

Whilst avoiding direct rent controls, these measures aim to increase transparency in the rental market. Tenants concerned about unfair practices might wish to familiarise themselves with these upcoming changes, whilst landlords may need to review their advertising and payment collection processes to ensure compliance.

The government maintains these reforms strike the right balance between tenant protections and maintaining private rental sector viability. With the first provisions taking effect in 2026, both renters and property owners have time to prepare for the new regulatory environment.

item.title: Government rules out rent controls
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government has confirmed it will not introduce rent controls in England, with housing secretary Angela Rayner stating the recently implemented Renters’ Rights Act provides sufficient protection for tenants. Speaking to the BBC, Rayner expressed scepticism about the effectiveness of rent controls, citing mixed results from schemes elsewhere in the UK.

Why rent controls have been ruled out

Rayner questioned whether rent controls actually reduce costs for tenants, pointing to Scotland’s temporary rent freeze between 2022 and 2023 as evidence that such measures may not deliver long-term solutions. The housing secretary emphasised that the Renters’ Rights Act – which came into force in May – already empowers tenants by limiting rent increases to once per year, tied to a property’s open market value.

This stance marks a shift from positions previously held by senior Labour figures. Prime minister Andy Burnham advocated for rent freezes during his tenure as Greater Manchester mayor in 2023, while former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn included rent controls in his 2019 election manifesto. Corbyn described the government’s decision as “extremely disappointing”, arguing that action on soaring rents remains essential to tackle homelessness.

Alternative approaches to rental reform

With rent controls off the table, ministers appear to be focusing on the Renters’ Rights Act as their primary mechanism for improving conditions in the private rented sector. The legislation introduces several tenant protections including:

  • Annual limits on rent increases
  • Stronger eviction safeguards
  • Improved property standards enforcement

Scotland is taking a different approach, with legislation allowing ministers to designate specific areas as rent control zones from 2027. However, the UK government seems unconvinced this model would work effectively in England, preferring to monitor the impact of existing reforms before considering further intervention.

For now, tenants and landlords in England can expect the rental market to continue operating without price caps, with policymakers banking on the Renters’ Rights Act to strike a balance between tenant protections and landlord interests.

item.title: Homeowners urged to brace for further price falls
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

London's property market continues to lag behind other UK regions, with new analysis suggesting average house prices in the capital could fall by nearly £5,000 before year-end. Research by House Buyer Bureau reveals London as the only region recording consistent monthly price declines over the past year, contrasting with modest growth elsewhere in England.

Regional price variations emerge

While England's overall property market showed 0.3% average monthly growth, London experienced 0.2% monthly declines according to UK House Price Index data. The South East remained largely stable, whilst northern regions demonstrated stronger performance. The North East led with 0.8% monthly growth, followed by Yorkshire and the Humber and the North West at 0.6%.

Projections based on two-year trends indicate London's average property price may drop from £552,655 to £547,889 by December 2026 – a 0.9% reduction. This would place values approximately £21,000 below the capital's peak average of £568,801 recorded in July 2025.

Navigating a shifting London market

Chris Hodgkinson, House Buyer Bureau's managing director, notes London's unusual position: "Unlike previous cycles where declines proved temporary, the capital's market appears to have lost momentum." This sustained downturn presents particular challenges for homeowners considering sales.

With prices potentially decreasing further, Hodgkinson suggests: "In a softening market, delaying sales in hope of recovery can prove costly. As values decline monthly, buyers grow more selective and negotiations become tougher." Many London sellers now prioritise certainty over holding out for potentially unachievable prices.

The analysis highlights how regional variations continue shaping the UK property landscape. Whilst northern markets show resilience, London's distinct challenges may require different strategies from homeowners and buyers alike. Monitoring local trends remains crucial when making property decisions in the current climate.

item.title: Cracks appear in Labour’s 1.5m homes pledge
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The government's ambitious pledge to build 1.5 million new homes in England during this parliamentary term is facing growing scrutiny, with Housing Secretary Angela Rayner admitting the target presents "a really difficult challenge". The admission comes as industry experts question whether current housebuilding rates can realistically meet this cornerstone manifesto commitment.

Stretching targets in a challenging market

Labour's housing target, requiring approximately 300,000 completions annually, was always an ambitious goal. Recent comments from Rayner suggest the government recognises the scale of the challenge, with the minister comparing it to training for a marathon. "I'm not dropping it - I'm just saying it's a really difficult challenge," Rayner told reporters, while maintaining the target remains in place.

Current market conditions present multiple obstacles including rising construction costs, planning delays and skills shortages. These factors have contributed to consistently missing annual housebuilding targets in recent years. With each shortfall, the cumulative target becomes harder to achieve as the required annual output increases in subsequent years.

Industry concerns and government response

Property developers and housing bodies have highlighted several structural barriers to delivering the government's target. Planning system backlogs, infrastructure constraints and economic viability pressures continue to limit building rates. Some industry analysts suggest the annual requirement would need to exceed 340,000 completions in the final years of parliament to compensate for early shortfalls.

Despite these challenges, ministers maintain their commitment to the overall target. Rayner has described it as a "stretched target" rather than an abandoned one, telling the BBC: "One-point-five million homes is a difficult target. It was when I made the target, but I'm going to keep the target, and I'm not going to be defeated." The government points to recent planning reforms and other measures designed to stimulate housing delivery.

For prospective homeowners and property investors, the ongoing debate highlights the complex interplay between political pledges and market realities in addressing the UK's chronic housing shortage. While the government's ambition is clear, its ability to overcome systemic barriers remains uncertain.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #446
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government has confirmed it has no plans to introduce rent controls in England, providing reassurance to landlords across the country. Deputy Prime Minister Angela Rayner made the announcement this week, stating that ministers would instead focus on strengthening tenant protections through existing regulations.

What the rent control decision means

The rejection of rent controls comes after months of speculation about potential government intervention in the private rental sector. Many landlords had expressed concerns that price caps could negatively impact their businesses and potentially reduce investment in rental properties.

Industry experts suggest this decision could help maintain stability in the private rental market. Without artificial price controls, landlords may feel more confident about maintaining their properties and potentially expanding their portfolios. However, tenant advocacy groups have voiced disappointment, arguing that more needs to be done to address affordability issues.

Alternative approaches to rental market reform

Rather than implementing rent controls, the government appears to be focusing on alternative measures to improve conditions for both landlords and tenants. These could include:

  • Strengthening enforcement of existing housing standards
  • Streamlining the eviction process for problem tenants while protecting good tenants
  • Encouraging longer tenancy agreements by default
  • Improving access to dispute resolution services

Property investors and landlords might wish to stay informed about these potential changes, as they could affect how rental properties are managed in future. The government's approach suggests a preference for market-led solutions rather than direct price intervention.

As the rental market continues to evolve, both landlords and tenants may benefit from keeping up with regulatory changes and understanding their respective rights and responsibilities under current legislation.
